**Entity SEO** in 2026 is the practice of establishing a brand as a discrete, machine-readable "thing" with verified attributes and relationships rather than a collection of keyword-matched "strings" [1-3]. Search engines and Large Language Models (LLMs) utilize **Knowledge Graphs**—structured databases of nodes and edges— to identify real-world objects and the facts connecting them [4-6]. Google’s Knowledge Graph currently holds over **1.6 trillion facts about 54 billion entities** [5, 7]. In a significant shift in June 2025, Google reportedly **pruned over three billion entities** in a single week, a move interpreted by third-party analysts as prioritizing a leaner dataset to improve the reliability of AI features [8-10].

LLMs build entity understanding through two distinct phases: **pre-training** on massive open corpora like Wikipedia, Wikidata, and Common Crawl, and **inference-time retrieval** where fresh web pages are reconciled against an internal entity model [11-14]. **Wikipedia** remains the highest-authority source because it simultaneously provides stable identifiers, an editorially filtered notability gate, and a cross-reference graph [15, 16]. **Wikidata** is often considered more achievable and equally critical, as its structured Q-number identifiers (e.g., Q42) serve as the backbone for both Wikipedia infoboxes and the Google Knowledge Graph [17-19]. The **`sameAs` schema property** is the primary technical lever for site owners, allowing them to link their on-site entity declaration (typically within an `Organization` or `Person` block) directly to these authoritative external IDs to ensure disambiguation [20-22].

The role of traditional backlinks has diminished in favor of **unlinked brand mentions** for AI visibility [23-25]. A 2025 **Semrush** study found that **branded web mentions correlate at 0.664** with AI Overview citations, compared to a significantly lower **0.218 correlation for traditional backlinks** [26, 27]. LLMs train on co-occurrence patterns, meaning that if a brand is consistently mentioned alongside a category across multiple credible editorial contexts, the model binds that brand vector tightly to that topic regardless of hyperlinks [25, 28, 29]. This has led to the emergence of **"vector real estate"** as a metaphor for brand authority, where mathematical proximity in a high-dimensional space determines citation frequency [30, 31].

**Query fan-out** is the core mechanism driving modern AI search, where a single user prompt is automatically expanded into **10 to 20 synthetic sub-queries** (and up to hundreds for "Deep Search" features) [32-34]. AI search queries have averaged **70–80 words**, representing a **17–26x increase in complexity** over traditional 3–4 word searches [35]. This mechanism means a brand with only one strong page on a broad topic will likely lose share to competitors who provide deep coverage across all fanned-out intent branches [36, 37]. Content must be structured as **self-contained answer units** of approximately **134–167 words** to be easily extracted by RAG (Retrieval-Augmented Generation) pipelines [38-40]. **Topic coverage** is the primary defense against fan-out instability; sites with **80%+ topical coverage** of their domain reportedly retain **85.4% of their AI visibility** even when fan-out sub-queries vary [41, 42].

**Disagreements and Evidence Notes:**
*   **Structured Data Necessity:** While vendor studies from **Princeton** and **Searchbloom** indicate that schema can boost visibility by **30–40%**, **Google's May 2026 AI search guide** states flatly that structured data is not a requirement to appear in AI Overviews [43-46].
*   **`llms.txt` Adoption:** Some agencies promote `llms.txt` as critical for GEO, but an **SE Ranking study** of 300,000 domains found only **10% adoption**, and Google advocates have publicly dismissed it as being similar to the obsolete "keywords" meta tag [47-49].
*   **Pruning Stats:** Data regarding the **three-billion-entity Knowledge Graph prune** and the **15.27% reduction in "Thing" entities** comes exclusively from a **vendor study by OutpaceSEO** [9, 10].

**Concrete 2026 Tactics and Tools:**
*   **Tactics:** Establish an **"Entity Home"** (usually an About page) containing a stable `@id` URI to avoid "data islands" [50-52]. Open informational sections with an entity definition in the first **40–60 words** [53-55]. Use **"Bottom Line Up Front" (BLUF)** writing styles to maximize extractability for RAG pipelines [55].
*   **Tools:** Monitor **Share of Model (SoM)** using tools like **LLM Pulse**, **Search Atlas LLM Visibility Tracker**, or **Otterly.ai** to track brand mention rates against competitors [56-59]. Use **Ahrefs Brand Radar** to identify specific fan-out queries being triggered for target topics [60, 61]. Validate entity strength using the **Google Knowledge Graph Search API** to monitor your entity's KGMID and confidence score [62-64].

Entity SEO is the practice of building your brand's presence so search engines and AI systems recognize it as a distinct, trusted entity in Google's Knowledge Graph — a database of more than 1.6 trillion facts about 54 billion entities ( Ahrefs, 2026 ). The Four Entity Types
With the authority foundation in place, the on-site work makes that authority machine-readable.

The sameAs property links your on-site entity declaration to external authoritative sources: your Wikidata entry, your Crunchbase profile, your verified LinkedIn company page. Think of it as cryptographic proof of identity. It lets an LLM merge your self-declared data with its pre-existing training knowledge of your brand. The more sameAs links you provide to trusted sources, the higher the confidence of the match. The mentions and about properties declare explicitly which entities are discussed within a given piece of content. Instead of making an AI crawler guess what your article is about by reading every word, you tell it directly. This removes ambiguity and dramatically improves extraction accuracy during RAG queries.

The signal mix has shifted, too. Per a 2025 Semrush analysis cited by Jottler , branded web mentions correlate more strongly with AI Overview citations than traditional backlinks — a meaningful reversal of the old link-first playbook. The same analysis reports that the large majority of AI Overview citations come from pages already ranking near the top of organic results, though the AI rarely simply picks the number-one result. Being widely and consistently mentioned now competes with, and often beats, being linked.

Your structured data, your sameAs links, your consistent entity definition across the web: these are not just SEO housekeeping. They are directly feeding the data structures that AI retrieval systems query in real time.

LLMs don't read the web by following links in real time. They train on massive static corpuses of text: Common Crawl, digitized books, Wikipedia, Reddit, curated web datasets. During this training, the model doesn't care whether your brand name has a hyperlink attached to it or not. What it cares about is co-occurrence and context. How often does your brand name appear near the concepts you want to be associated with? What kind of language surrounds those mentions? Is it positive, negative, or neutral?

Knowledge graph SEO is the practice of getting your entities (brand, people, products, concepts) recognized, disambiguated, and connected inside Google's Knowledge Graph and the broader entity layer that LLMs train on. It is not a tactic. It is the substrate everything else now runs on.

Entity-based search replaced string-based search around 2013, when Google rolled out Hummingbird. Every algorithm update since (RankBrain in 2015, BERT in 2019, MUM in 2021, the AI Overviews launch in 2024) has pushed Google further from matching keyword strings and closer to matching entity intent. A page can rank for "running shoes" without containing the phrase if Google understands the entities the page covers.

A study of 75,000 brands found that branded web mentions correlate most strongly with brand mentions in AI Overviews. Not backlink profiles. Not Domain Rating. Mentions, in context, across the open web. An LLM builds confidence from consensus. If ten independent sources discuss your brand favorably in the context of a specific product category, the model binds your brand vector tightly to that category.
Vector real estate: the spatial metaphor that makes this click

The phrase circulating in technical marketing circles is “vector real estate.” You earn it through semantic density: the frequency with which your brand name co-occurs with your target topic vocabulary across credible, diverse sources. The more consistent and widespread that co-occurrence, the tighter your vector clusters around those concepts, and the more reliably you get retrieved.

Query Reception and Context Retrieval The process begins with receiving a user's query, which can be typed, spoken, image-based, or multimodal. The input is processed, based on type, including ML models applied to convert non-text input (e.g. images) to machine-readable formats (e.g. for images – captioning, object detection, or semantically rich embeddings)

The behavior is consistent across the industry. Most AI-powered search engines, including Google's AI Overviews, AI Mode, Gemini, ChatGPT, Perplexity, Microsoft Copilot, and Grok, use query fan-out expansion methods to answer user prompts. The reasoning is practical: a single keyword-style search can't reliably cover all the angles of an open-ended question.

The Query Fan-Out Mechanism

The fan-out mechanism also shows why scattered breadth fails. A brand with one page each across 25 unrelated topics has no topical entity to pull against. Each query's fan-out pulls from a different topic. The brand wins on none of them. It has not built deep coverage in any neighborhood. Depth before breadth is not a preference. It is the only setup that works with query fan-out.

Topical coverage is the real defense against fan-out instability

You optimize for coverage rather than individual sub-queries. Fan-out queries are unstable, but sites with 80%+ topical coverage of their domain retain about 85.4% of their AI visibility despite roughly 73% query instability. Build comprehensive topic clusters, structure content into self-contained passages, add quantified specifics, and implement schema, which can raise selection probability by around 73%.
The Princeton GEO Study

AI systems pull and tag content by entity, not by keyword. Entity work compounds. The retrieval index sees a brand, a person, a product, or a topic as one entity, and then tracks each entity's authority signals across the open web because the same entity surfaces across many subqueries within a single user prompt. Entity work makes the four types into clean retrieval targets. The four types are brand, people, products and services, and topical. This chapter covers six core moves. First, how entity recognition works. Second, query fan-out, which makes entity work pay off across many queries at once. Third, depth before breadth for topical entities. Fourth, the Knowledge Panel claim. Fifth, Wikidata and Wikipedia work. Sixth, the named-expert pattern, which turns founders into entities that can be cited.

You cannot skip traditional SEO and jump to GEO. The AI reads the top results. If you're not in the top 10, you're statistically unlikely to be read by the AI in the first place.

LLM citation behaviour favours recognized entities. When Claude or Perplexity generates an answer, it preferentially cites sources whose publisher is a known entity over those whose publisher is ambiguous.

The other architectural shift is “Bottom Line Up Front” writing. AI crawlers prefer content where the definitive answer appears in the first 40 to 60 words after a heading. Those compact, self-contained answer blocks are what get extracted as citation blocks in RAG pipelines. FAQPage schema amplifies this dramatically. Adding FAQPage schema to your key pages is declaring to every AI crawler: here are the questions this page answers, and here are the precise answers.

How does each visibility tool report? Search Atlas LLM Visibility tracker runs branded and unbranded prompts against ChatGPT, Claude, Perplexity, Gemini, and Google AI Overviews, then records mentions, citations, sentiment, and share of voice. Profound and AthenaHQ provide similar coverage with their own prompt sets.

Tracking these requires dedicated tools. The market has moved fast. Platforms like LLM Pulse, Peec AI, Profound, and Kime autonomously query multiple LLMs repeatedly to extract quantitative performance data. They track your brand across ChatGPT, Gemini, Perplexity, and Claude simultaneously, giving you the visibility data that web analytics platforms completely miss.

AI systems and search engines alike prioritize content from trusted sources that demonstrate real expertise. When algorithms evaluate content — whether for search rankings, featured snippets, or AI-generated answers — they’re increasingly sophisticated at detecting these E-E-A-T signals.

Share of model (SoM) . As we defined above, this is your mention share versus competitors in AI answers. Track this across each platform separately — only 11% of domains are cited by both ChatGPT and Perplexity , according to CiteMetrix’s analysis of 680 million tracked AI citations. Even within Google’s own products, AI Overviews and AI Mode share only 13.7% of their cited URLs . What works on one platform may not work on another.
